已知最早的庫姆茲類樂器可追溯至四世紀；相關亞塞拜然戈普茲則有約公元前六千年陶板圖: The earliest known instruments of the komuz type go back to the fourth century; the related Azerbaijani gopuz appears on a clay tablet of about 6000 BC. It reached the Xiongnu before the Han dynasty, was presented as tribute to the Tang emperor and then passed on to Japan; in the thirteenth century, when Genghis Khan campaigned westward, it spread to Badakhshan, Kashmir, Central Asia, Persia and Arabia. In the fourth and fifth centuries it also entered Ukraine, Poland and Hungary with the migrations of the Huns. In the Soviet period it was considered crude and frets were added; after independence it returned to the conservatories.

The three strings have no frets, and the tuning can be chosen to suit the tune. Start practice with a simple melody, playing it over and again with a new right-hand pattern each time, to train technique and inventiveness. The more advanced can try playing with the instrument on the shoulder or behind the head.

It is mostly held across the body while seated, plucked or strummed. Representative pieces include “The Nightingale”, “The Woodpecker on the Pine” and “The Bay Chestnut Foal”.

The komuz is an ancient Central Asian plucked instrument without frets, a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.321, related to the plucked instruments of Turkic-speaking peoples, to the Mongolian tovshuur and to the lute. The body is mostly made from a single piece of wood, traditionally with three strings, gut early on and more recently fishing line or silk; it is mostly held across the body while seated, plucked or strummed, and also laid on the leg, the shoulder or behind the head. Turkic-speaking peoples such as the Kyrgyz use it for the akyn's sung recitation, for chanting epics, for folk music, and for accompaniment or solo playing.
庫姆茲琴通常以整塊木頭製成，常見杏木或杜松；中國柯爾克孜族傳統多選紅松，因稀缺改: The komuz is usually made from a single piece of wood, commonly apricot or juniper; the Kyrgyz of China traditionally chose Korean pine, and because it is scarce now use cypress, fruit wood, mulberry or apricot. The soundbox is slightly flat and close to pear-shaped, the head oval and the neck slender. The sounding part is the three strings, mostly gut early on and more recently silk or fishing line. The pegs sit in a row on one side. The thickness of the top and the setting up of the strings are done by experience. The source does not state the materials of the other parts.
庫姆茲琴音色醇厚，音域寬廣；以三弦彈撥發聲，可撥奏或掃弦，常見調音中中弦音高最高: The komuz has a full, mellow timbre and a broad range; it sounds from three plucked strings, plucked or strummed, and in the common tuning the middle string is the highest. It is held across the body, on the leg, the shoulder or behind the head, and is used for solos, duets, call-and-answer playing, ensembles and accompaniment. The source does not say how the volume is controlled; as for how it differs from related instruments, the source says only that it is a fretless three-string instrument, unlike the related bowed kobyz.
